summary: Analyzes common security threats to OLSRv2 and their effects on mobile ad hoc networks, and which are mitigated by the mandatory-to-implement security mechanisms.

eli5.summary: A list of ways the bad guys could mess up a roaming radio network and which are stopped.

subtitle: Security vulnerabilities in mobile ad hoc network routing and how to mitigate them.

tldr.problem: The Optimized Link State Routing Protocol Version 2 (OLSRv2) is designed for mobile ad hoc networks, but wireless networks lack the physical constraints of wired networks, making them vulnerable to attacks by compromised routers injecting false routing information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8116 identifies three categories of threats: attacks that prevent topology map acquisition, attacks that cause incorrect topology maps, and attacks that create inconsistent topology views across the network. It also details which vulnerabilities can be mitigated by the mandatory RFC 7183 security mechanisms.
tldr.outcome: By understanding these threats and deploying RFC 7183 security protections, OLSRv2 networks can be hardened against compromised routers that attempt to disrupt routing.

today: RFC 8116 is an Informational RFC published in May 2017. It is not obsoleted or updated. It serves as a security analysis reference for OLSRv2 deployments, documenting known vulnerabilities and guiding the use of RFC 7183 security mechanisms in MANET routing networks.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.content:
OLSRv2 is a routing protocol for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs), which are networks of wireless devices (routers) that communicate without fixed infrastructure. As these networks have grown in real-world deployments, such as the FunkFeuer community networks, the assumption that all participants will behave honestly has become unrealistic. RFC 8116 analyzes the security vulnerabilities inherent in OLSRv2 and evaluates which can be mitigated using mandatory security mechanisms.

OLSRv2 operates through three basic processes: neighborhood discovery (NHDP), Multipoint Relay (MPR) selection for efficient flooding, and Link State Advertisements (LSAs) that propagate routing information. Attacks typically involve a compromised router either eavesdropping on network traffic or injecting syntactically correct but invalid control messages (HELLO and TC messages).
sections.eli5: OLSRv2 is a routing system for wireless radio networks. Bad routers can pretend to be good ones and mess up the directions that packets follow. This document explains what tricks they use.

sections.title: Topology Map Acquisition Attacks
sections.content:
Topology map acquisition attacks prevent routers from learning about the network structure. One attack targets the jittering mechanism: OLSRv2 adds random delays to control messages to reduce collisions. A compromised router can send many messages in quick succession, overwhelming the jitter mechanism and causing its false messages to arrive first, preempting legitimate ones with the same message ID.

Another class of attacks manipulates the hop limit or hop count fields in messages. Because these fields change during message forwarding, they are not protected by integrity checks. A compromised router can decrease the hop limit to restrict how far a message spreads, or modify the hop count to affect validity time calculations. This can cause routers to expire or discard legitimate routing information prematurely.
sections.eli5: One trick is to flood the network with messages so fast that a bad router's lies arrive before the truth. Another trick is to mess with message fields that don't have protection, making routers forget good routing information too quickly.

sections.title: Effective Topology Attacks
sections.content:
Effective topology attacks cause routers to build incorrect maps that do not reflect actual network connectivity. One attack is incorrect forwarding: a router can participate in routing protocols but refuse to forward data traffic. Other routers believe they can reach destinations through this router, but packets are silently dropped, disconnecting parts of the network.

Wormhole attacks create an illusion of a direct link between distant routers by relaying control messages through a hidden, out-of-band channel. Sequence number attacks exploit OLSRv2's use of two sequence numbers: a Message Sequence Number prevents duplicate processing, but a compromised router can spoof another router's identity and transmit messages with high sequence numbers, preventing legitimate future messages from that router from being accepted.

Indirect jamming causes legitimate routers to generate excessive control traffic. A compromised router flips the advertised link status of its neighbors between 'MPR' and 'LOST' states. Each change triggers topology recalculation in all network routers, causing continuous processing overhead and potentially exhausting battery-powered devices.
sections.eli5: Bad routers can pretend to forward traffic but secretly drop it. They can create fake shortcuts. They can steal another router's identity and flood the network with messages. They can also trick routers into constantly recalculating routes by pretending to change.

sections.title: Inconsistent Topology Attacks
sections.content:
Identity spoofing occurs when a compromised router claims to be another router. Via LSA, it can advertise links under another router's identity, causing the network to split into partitions: some routers believe they can reach a destination through one path, while others believe they must use a different (longer or nonexistent) path. The attack is particularly difficult to counter because the malicious router uses legitimate MPR selectors to distribute false information.

Link spoofing advertises non-existent links, making routers believe there are paths that do not actually exist. This similarly partitions the network: routers on one side of the false link reach destinations through the legitimate path, while routers on the other side are directed toward the spoofed link and become disconnected.

Both attacks result in multiple routers maintaining substantially different topology maps, causing traffic for the same destination to be routed inconsistently across the network.
sections.eli5: A bad router can steal another router's name and tell everyone it has connections it doesn't have. This tricks the network into thinking there are shortcuts that don't exist, splitting the network apart so some routers can't reach each other.

sections.title: Security Mitigation Mechanisms
sections.content:
OLSRv2 provides some inherent resilience without additional security measures: it uses message sequence numbers to reject old or duplicate messages, detects and ignores unidirectional links, and imposes message interval bounds that limit some attack effects. However, these are insufficient against determined attackers.

RFC 7183 specifies mandatory-to-implement security mechanisms for OLSRv2 using HMAC/SHA-256 integrity checks and timestamps for replay protection. Each control message receives an Integrity Check Value (ICV) computed over a shared key. A router without valid credentials cannot generate a correct ICV, so its messages are rejected by legitimate routers. This prevents identity spoofing, link spoofing, and sequence number attacks because any modification of control messages would invalidate the ICV.

RFC 7183 protection is highly effective but requires a shared key among all routers in the MANET. Deployments must carefully manage key distribution and rotation. The document notes that while RFC 7183 is mandatory to implement, alternative security mechanisms (such as IPsec on lower layers) may be more appropriate for specific deployments.
sections.eli5: OLSRv2 has some built-in defenses, but they are not enough. A real security fix uses a shared secret key: each router signs its messages so others know they are real. If a bad router tries to forge a message, the signature fails and other routers ignore it.
